title: Should timers be ordered by scheduled time or by passed millis?

labels.name: interop
labels.description: Implementations are not interoperable with each other

body:
From this [StackOverlow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/72737324/) it was brought to my attention that there currently is an interop issue regarding the ordering of timers that get executed after all their scheduled is expired.  

Given a code that does ([jsfiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/w3e1Lfv7/))

```js
setTimeout(fn1, 100);
blockTheEventLoopFor(200);
setTimeout(fn2, 0);
blockTheEventLoopFor(20); // avoid the 1ms clamping in Chrome
```
Firefox, Safari, and the current stable branch of Chrome all will execute `fn1` then `fn2`.  
Using `t=0` as the global time at the start of the script, the logic here seems to be, `fn1` is scheduled to fire at `0 + 100`, then `fn2` is scheduled to fire at `200 + 0` and when the event loop gains control again at `t=220`, it calls both callbacks in the scheduled time order. Makes sense to me.  

But now, the previous stable Chrome version, and the current beta, dev, and canary branches actually call `fn2` then `fn1`.  
And to my surprise, this is also what the specs ask for.

Indeed, in the step 5.2 of [run steps after a timeout](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/timers-and-user-prompts.html#run-steps-after-a-timeout), it is asked to 

> Wait until any invocations of this algorithm that had the same global and orderingIdentifier, that started before this one, and whose ***milliseconds*** is equal to or less than this one's, have completed.

(emphasize mine)

So when the event loop gains control again at `t=220`, both `fn1` and `fn2` are scheduled to be called, but given that `fn2` has a lower "milliseconds", it's actually this one that get chosen. Which is IMO particularly surprising.  

I'm thus wondering if "milliseconds" here should be changed to "*startTime* plus *milliseconds*" or "map of active timers[timerKey]" (, or its own variable)?
